opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of those things that sounds like a technicality but actually matters a lot once you try to train a model on Go.

When humans finish a game, they don't play it out until every stone is literally captured. They both look at the board and agree that a group is dead, even though it's still sitting there, because it has no realistic way to make two eyes. Under Japanese rules you then remove those stones and count territory. That works fine between two strong players who share an understanding of life and death. But it hides a lot of judgment. Sometimes a group is only "dead" if you read out a long sequence correctly, and there are weird edge cases like seki or ko situations where reasonable people disagree. Historically there have been real disputes in professional games over exactly this.

For a computer, that's a nightmare, because the reward signal at the end of the game depends on a judgment the system is supposed to be learning in the first place. So in practice most AI work uses something like Tromp-Taylor rules: area scoring, where you count your stones plus the empty points only you surround, and nothing is removed unless it's actually captured. The game continues until both players pass, and if you think a group is dead, you have to prove it by capturing it. It's unambiguous and fully mechanical. The cost is the games get a bit longer and uglier, but the score is a pure function of the board.

What I find interesting is the tension that creates. A network trained under strict rules is arguably more honest, because it can't rely on social agreement. But you also see strange behavior. The well-known adversarial attacks on KataGo exploited this. The bot would think it had won because, by human intuition, the opponent's stones in its territory were dead, so it passed. Under strict scoring, those stones were never captured, so they counted, and the bot lost to a pretty weak strategy. It learned a value function that was "mostly right" in the human sense, but the actual rules disagreed with it at the margins.

To me that's a nice small-scale picture of a bigger problem in machine learning. A lot of real-world objectives look like Japanese scoring: there's a shared, fuzzy notion of what counts, and humans resolve ambiguity through agreement. When you formalize it into a reward function, you have to pick something mechanical like Tromp-Taylor, and the model then optimizes the literal rule, including the corners you didn't think about. So the Go scoring question is really a question about how you specify what you want in a way that's both precise and still means what you meant.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of my favorite little corners of Go, because it's a place where the game itself admits that the rules aren't fully formal. In chess you never have to negotiate whether the game is over. In Go you literally do. At the end, both players pass, and then you have to agree on which stones are dead and which are alive, and the scoring depends on that agreement.

The interesting thing is that the "correct" answer is well-defined in principle. If a group is dead, that means that if you played it out to the end, with the attacker trying to capture and the defender trying to save it, the defender would lose. So dead-ness is really a counterfactual claim about a game tree you didn't actually play. Humans resolve this through a kind of social protocol: if you disagree, you resume the game and actually play it out, usually under rules that don't penalize the player for the extra moves. So the ambiguity gets collapsed by just running the simulation.

What I find fascinating from the machine learning side is that this is a nice illustration of the difference between a reward that's computable and a reward that's merely decidable. The Tromp-Taylor rules make it fully computable: you don't recognize dead stones at all, you just play everything out until every stone is either captured or unambiguously alive. That's clean, and it's why basically every Go engine, including the AlphaGo lineage, trains on that rule set internally. But humans hate playing that way because it's tedious. You're filling in moves that any competent player already knows the outcome of.

So the human rule set is essentially a compression of Tromp-Taylor, where you skip the boring part because both agents share enough world knowledge to agree on the outcome. The ambiguity only shows up when the two models disagree, and the resolution is to fall back to the uncompressed version.

I think that pattern generalizes way beyond Go. A lot of what we call "ambiguity" in evaluating agents, or in RLHF-style reward, is exactly this: we have an expensive ground-truth procedure, and a cheap heuristic that two parties usually agree on, and the ambiguity is just the gap between them. When the heuristic fails, you don't want to argue about it. You want a mechanism to escalate to the expensive thing. Go has had that mechanism built in for centuries, and I think that's kind of beautiful.

The one place where it genuinely does get philosophically weird is seki and some of the edge cases with no-territory situations under Japanese rules, where even strong players can disagree about what the score "should" be because the rules encode a lot of history and aesthetic judgment rather than pure game-theoretic outcome. That's a case where the compression isn't lossless, and the rules are sort of papering over it with precedent. Which, again, feels like a very familiar situation if you've ever tried to write an evaluation rubric.

r001.rationale: The response explains dead stones as a counterfactual capture outcome and discusses resuming play, but does not state that connecting the surrounded white group to something outside the enclosing black formation can overturn its assessment as dead.

astra-6.text:
The interesting thing is that a stone being surrounded doesn’t necessarily mean it’s dead. The question is whether it can avoid capture if you actually play things out. And that can require a surprisingly deep understanding of the position.

So when two experienced players agree to remove dead stones at the end, they’re implicitly agreeing on a counterfactual: “We could keep playing, and we both know how this would end.” They skip that computation because they agree on the result. If they disagree, you need a procedure for resolving it, and the details depend on the ruleset.

I think that’s a useful distinction: the rules can be precise while applying them efficiently still requires intelligence. The ambiguity is often in the players’ understanding of what would happen, rather than in whether the stones are literally surrounded.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a nice example of how even a game with very precise rules can have this layer of implicit understanding. A group being surrounded doesn’t necessarily mean it’s dead. The question is whether it can survive if you actually play things out.

Experienced players can usually agree on that without playing all the extra moves. They’re essentially saying, “We both know how this continuation goes, so let’s skip it.” But if they disagree, there are procedures for continuing play and resolving it, depending on the ruleset.

So I’d distinguish ambiguity in the rules from uncertainty about the consequences of the rules. You can have a perfectly well-defined outcome that’s still difficult to determine without doing a lot of computation. The agreement between players is a shortcut around that computation.
